title: Tanker hit by projectile leaving Hormuz as third US carrier arrives; Iran claims six ships sunk
dek: A maritime monitor says a tanker caught fire after being struck on Monday morning. Iran's Guards say six vessels have burned or sunk since Saturday and warn ships off a US-backed route; none of their claims has been independently confirmed.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
A tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile while leaving the Strait of Hormuz on Monday morning, setting off a fire in its engine room, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) said, as a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the region and Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned shipowners against using what they called a US-backed route through the strait. UKMTO said the incident took place at 05.58 GMT (11.28 am IST), that no casualties had been reported and that all crew were accounted for; the extent of the damage and any environmental impact were not yet known. It did not name the vessel or its flag.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says six vessels have caught fire or sunk in the strait since Saturday, including a supertanker it said sank on Sunday with more than two million barrels of crude on board. No shipowner, flag state or maritime monitor has confirmed those figures, and US President Donald Trump has accused Iran of exaggerating ship incidents to push up oil prices, according to reports.

## Monday: a third carrier and new threats

The USS Theodore Roosevelt entered the area of US Central Command on Sunday, joining the carriers USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, according to reports. In a statement carried by the IRGC's news outlet, its navy described the southern route that the US has said is clear for shipping as a "minefield of fire" and said shipowners who trusted American assurances would become "prey to the flames", reports said. It described its actions as a response to an "illegal American blockade" of Iranian ports. Iran's regular army separately said on Monday that another tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine east of the strait; it was not clear whether that was the vessel UKMTO reported.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Monday that the "neither peace nor war" situation between Iran and the US had to end and called for a "serious diplomatic process of negotiation", according to reports. Qatar and Saudi Arabia condemned Sunday's Iranian drone attack on Bahrain, and the Gulf Cooperation Council's secretary-general, Jasem Al Budaiwi, called it a "blatant challenge" to regional peace efforts, reports said.

## Sunday: the supertanker claim

The IRGC said on Sunday that a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil had sunk after striking a mine in the southern waters of the Gulf, near the Strait of Hormuz. Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO), which monitors shipping in the region, said Indian shipping authorities had reported an attack on a tanker in the Gulf just before the strait, and that the crew were accounted for and safe.

There was no independent confirmation of the sinking. UKMTO said it was not clear whether the attack reported by the Indian authorities was the same incident the IRGC described, and that the extent of damage to the vessel and any environmental impact were not yet known.

## What each side said

In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the IRGC said two tankers had hit mines while travelling on what it called an "unauthorised route" in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, and that one of them, a supertanker, had caught fire and sunk. It did not name the vessels, their owners or their flags. On Saturday, the IRGC's navy had said two tankers struck mines after switching off their tracking systems, and that two others turned back after warnings from its maritime traffic control centre, according to Iran's official news agency.

UKMTO said the tanker in the Indian report was eastbound in the Gulf, before entering the strait, when it was attacked. It advised vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity. India's shipping authorities had not published details of the vessel, its flag or its crew by early Monday.

Iran says only Iran and Oman have the right to control traffic through the strait and requires ships to use routes it authorises. The United States rejects that claim, has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and has escorted tankers through the waterway. The US military said recently that it had cleared mines from the main shipping routes, according to reports.

The army's public relations office said the tanker it reported on Monday had been violating Iran's maritime rules and had switched off its navigation systems, according to Iranian state media; it did not name the ship or say whether anyone was hurt.

## Why it matters for India

About a fifth of the world's oil normally passes through the Strait of Hormuz, and a large share of India's crude and cooking gas imports come from Gulf producers whose cargoes use it. Indian seafarers make up a large part of the crews on tankers and cargo ships in the region. On 3 November an Indian national was killed when the Indian vessel MSV Al Jusufi was attacked off Limah in Oman; 13 other Indians on board were rescued, the Ministry of External Affairs said at the time.

The latest incidents follow two days in which the IRGC said it had attacked US radar installations in Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. The US military said it shot down the two drones launched on Friday, and Bahrain said its air defences intercepted the attacks on Sunday. The IRGC repeated on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz "is closed".

## What happens next

Shipping companies and insurers will be watching for the identities of the vessels from tracking data, owners or flag states. Brent crude traded at about $95-96 a barrel on Monday, according to reports, as forecasts of a global supply surplus offset the risk to shipping. Iran has set out seven conditions for a deal with the United States through a Qatari mediator, including lifting the naval blockade and sanctions, and is awaiting a US response, according to reports.
